parts.title: Reading Passage 1
parts.instruction: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13.
parts.content:
THE RETURN OF THE URBAN ORCHARD

For most of the twentieth century, fruit trees disappeared from the centres of European cities. Orchards that had once supplied town markets were sold for housing, and the few trees that survived in parks were often cut down because falling fruit was considered a nuisance. By 1980, a survey in the Dutch city of Utrecht found fewer than two hundred fruit trees on public land, most of them over fifty years old.

The change began quietly. In the late 1990s, a group of residents in Utrecht asked the council for permission to plant apple and pear trees on a strip of unused land beside a railway line. The council agreed, partly because the residents promised to look after the trees themselves. Within ten years the strip held more than sixty trees, and the idea had spread to other neighbourhoods.

Supporters of urban orchards point to several benefits. Fruit trees provide food for bees and other insects at a time of year when few other plants are flowering. Their roots help rainwater soak into the ground instead of running into overloaded drains. And, according to a study by Wageningen University, people who live within three hundred metres of a community orchard report feeling more connected to their neighbours than those who do not.

There are difficulties, however. Fruit trees need pruning every winter, and many councils lack staff with the necessary skills. Some early projects failed because volunteers lost interest after the first harvest. Others ran into trouble when nobody had agreed who owned the fruit: in one case in Hamburg, a local restaurant began picking the cherries before residents could reach them, leading to a dispute that took two years to settle.

To avoid such problems, most successful projects now use a written agreement. This normally states who is responsible for pruning, how the harvest will be shared, and what happens if the group stops meeting. Several cities, including Ghent and Malmö, have published model agreements that new groups can adapt.

The choice of tree also matters. Old local varieties are often more resistant to disease than modern commercial ones, and they need fewer chemical sprays. Nurseries that specialise in these varieties have seen demand rise sharply; one in Belgium reports that sales to community groups have tripled since 2015. Experts also recommend planting a mix of early and late varieties, so that fruit is available from July to October rather than all at once.

Not everyone is convinced. Critics argue that a few hundred trees can make no real difference to a city's food supply, and that the money would be better spent on larger parks. Supporters accept that orchards will never feed a city, but say that this was never the point. "An orchard is a reason for people to meet," says Marieke de Vries, who helped plant the first Utrecht trees. "The fruit is a bonus."

parts.title: Reading Passage 2
parts.instruction: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26.
parts.content:
HOW BRIDGES LEARNED TO MOVE

A. In 2000, thousands of people walked across London's new Millennium Bridge on its opening day. Within minutes the bridge began to sway from side to side, and walkers instinctively adjusted their steps to keep their balance. Their movement made the swaying worse. The bridge was closed two days later and did not reopen for almost two years.

B. Engineers had known for a long time that soldiers should break step when crossing a bridge, because marching in time can make a structure vibrate. What surprised them in London was that ordinary walkers, who had no reason to move together, fell into step without meaning to. The bridge's sideways movement, although small at first, was enough to make hundreds of people shift their weight at the same moment.

C. The solution was not to make the bridge heavier or stiffer, which would have spoiled its slim design. Instead, engineers fitted it with dampers - devices that absorb energy, working in a similar way to the shock absorbers in a car. Ninety-one dampers were installed under the deck and around the supports. Tests with up to two thousand volunteers showed that the bridge now stayed almost still.

D. The London case changed how footbridges are designed around the world. Before 2000, most design codes considered only the vertical forces produced by walking. Today, engineers must also check how a bridge will respond to sideways forces, and many now run computer models of crowds before a design is approved. The cost of these checks is small compared with the cost of closing a bridge after it opens.

E. Some engineers have gone further and designed bridges that are meant to move. In parts of Japan, bridges are built on bearings that allow them to slide during an earthquake, so that the ground can shake beneath them without tearing the structure apart. Similar ideas are used in tall buildings, where heavy weights near the top swing in the opposite direction to the wind.

F. Despite these advances, engineers admit that crowds remain hard to predict. People walk differently when they are excited, when they are carrying bags, or when they are in a hurry. One researcher compares designing for crowds to forecasting the weather: models are improving every year, but there will always be some uncertainty. For this reason, most new footbridges are now tested with real crowds before they open to the public.

parts.title: Reading Passage 3
parts.instruction: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40.
parts.content:
THE VALUE OF BOREDOM

Boredom has a poor reputation. Parents work hard to keep children entertained, employers worry about staff who seem uninterested, and many adults reach for their phones the moment they have nothing to do. Yet a growing number of psychologists argue that boredom is not simply an unpleasant feeling to be avoided, but a signal that serves a useful purpose.

According to this view, boredom works rather like hunger. Hunger tells us that we need food; boredom tells us that what we are doing no longer meets our needs, and pushes us to look for something more rewarding. Dr Erin Westgate of the University of Florida describes it as "a message that our attention is not being well used". On this account, the problem is not boredom itself but what we do in response to it.

Some research suggests that boredom can even encourage creative thinking. In a well-known experiment at the University of Central Lancashire, Sandi Mann asked one group of volunteers to copy numbers from a telephone directory for fifteen minutes, while a second group did nothing beforehand. Both groups were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. The volunteers who had first done the dull copying task produced more ideas, and their ideas were judged to be more original.

Mann's findings have been widely reported, but other researchers urge caution. The experiment was small, and later studies have produced mixed results. James Danckert, who studies boredom at the University of Waterloo, points out that boredom can also lead people to make poor choices, such as eating unhealthy snacks or taking unnecessary risks. In his view, boredom is useful only if people respond to it by finding something meaningful to do.

There is also disagreement about whether modern life is making people more bored. Some writers claim that smartphones have reduced our ability to cope with even a few minutes of inactivity. Danckert is less sure. He notes that people have always complained of boredom, and that there is little reliable data comparing levels of boredom today with those of fifty years ago. What does seem clear is that constant entertainment does not cure boredom; surveys suggest that heavy users of social media report feeling bored more often, not less.

For parents and teachers, the research offers some practical lessons. Children who are given time without planned activities may learn to invent their own games and to tolerate frustration. Several schools in Finland have experimented with short periods each week in which pupils choose freely what to do, and teachers report that pupils become better at organising themselves. However, the researchers stress that unstructured time is not the same as neglect: children still need adults who can suggest ideas when they get stuck.

Perhaps the most important lesson is that boredom is a normal part of life. Rather than trying to eliminate it, we might do better to listen to what it is telling us.
